subject: Geography
name: Geography, Year 9
about: Australian Curriculum, Year 9: Biomes and food security, Geographies of interconnections
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Reading a climate graph
points.brief: A climate graph shows a place's average rainfall each month as columns and its average temperature as a line, so you can read its wet and dry, hot and cool seasons.

points.title: Choropleth maps
points.brief: A choropleth map shades areas from light to dark to show how much of something each area has, such as crop yield or internet access.

points.title: Flow maps
points.brief: A flow map uses arrows to show movement between places, with thicker arrows for larger flows, such as trade or tourists.

points.title: Layers in a GIS
points.brief: A geographical information system stores data as map layers, such as soils, rainfall and roads, which can be laid over each other to find patterns.

points.title: What a biome is
points.brief: A biome is a large region with a similar climate, soils, plants and animals, such as a tropical rainforest or a desert.

points.title: Land biomes
points.brief: The main land biomes are tropical rainforest, temperate forest, savanna, grassland, desert and tundra, each found in a band set mostly by climate.

points.title: Water biomes
points.brief: Aquatic biomes are marine, such as oceans and coral reefs, or freshwater, such as rivers, lakes and wetlands.

points.title: Biome productivity
points.brief: Warm, wet biomes such as rainforests grow the most plant matter each year. Cold or dry biomes such as tundra and desert grow the least.

points.title: The spheres and biomes
points.brief: Biomes depend on the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere working together, so human activities that change one, such as clearing or mining, change the biome.

points.title: Food and fibre from biomes
points.brief: Grasslands grow wheat and graze sheep and cattle, rainforests give fruit, coffee, rubber and palm oil, and oceans give fish.

points.title: Natural and farmed ecosystems
points.brief: A farm has fewer species than the natural biome it replaced, and its nutrients and water are added and taken away by people rather than cycling naturally.

points.title: Changing biomes to grow more
points.brief: Irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides, new seed varieties and terracing let people grow more food than the natural biome would allow.

points.title: Environmental factors in farming
points.brief: Climate, soil, landform and water decide what can be grown where, such as wheat on Australia's dry plains and rice on Asia's wet river deltas.

points.title: Economic factors in farming
points.brief: Farm output depends on land, labour, money to invest, and access to storage, transport and markets.

points.title: Technology in farming
points.brief: Satellite mapping, GIS, sensors and new crop varieties help farmers put water and fertiliser where needed and lift yields.

points.title: Farming innovations
points.brief: Drip irrigation, crop rotation, stubble mulching, intercropping and drought-resistant crops reduce the limits the environment puts on food production.

points.title: What food security means
points.brief: Food security means everyone can always get enough safe, healthy food. It depends on how much food is grown, whether people can afford it and whether it reaches them.

points.title: Land degradation
points.brief: Soil erosion, salinity and desertification lower how much farmland can grow, and they are often caused by clearing, overgrazing and poor irrigation.

points.title: Pressures on future food supply
points.brief: Climate change, water shortages and cities spreading onto farmland all threaten how much food can be grown.

points.title: Bush foods and changed biomes
points.brief: Clearing and grazing reduced bush foods First Nations Australians relied on, such as the yam daisy (myrrnong) in Victoria. Some bush foods are now grown and sold.

points.title: Improving food security
points.brief: Cutting food waste, caring for soil, trade and research into new crops all help make sure there is enough food in future.

points.title: Transport and access
points.brief: Roads, flights and public transport decide how easily people reach jobs, services and other places, which changes how they use and see a place.

points.title: Supply chains
points.brief: A supply chain is every step a product takes from raw material to buyer, such as cotton grown, spun, sewn into a T-shirt, shipped and sold.

points.title: The digital divide
points.brief: Internet access is uneven between and within countries, with remote and poorer areas often left with slow or no connection.

points.title: Services across borders
points.brief: Fast internet lets businesses provide services from far away, such as call centres in India and the Philippines serving Australian customers.

points.title: Growth of tourism
points.brief: Cheaper flights, higher incomes and the internet have made tourism one of the world's largest industries.

points.title: Impacts of tourism
points.brief: Tourism brings jobs and money but can crowd places, damage environments and change local cultures.

points.title: Managing tourism at Uluru-Kata Tjuta
points.brief: Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is jointly managed by Anangu Traditional Owners and Parks Australia. Climbing Uluru was closed in 2019 out of respect for its cultural meaning.

points.title: Trade links places
points.brief: Places are linked by buying and selling goods and services at every scale, from a local shop to global exports.

points.title: Changing trade links
points.brief: Trade connections change over time. Australia once traded mostly with Britain and now trades mostly with Asia.

points.title: How production affects places
points.brief: Mining, farming, forestry and factories change the places that make goods, through jobs, pollution and cleared land.

points.title: E-waste and a product's life
points.brief: A phone's life runs from mining metals to making, selling and throwing it away. Its e-waste often ends up in poorer countries where it harms health and land.

points.title: Managing waste sustainably
points.brief: Reducing, reusing and recycling, and laws making businesses take back old products, cut the harm waste does to places.
